cards.title: The fall of Constantinople
cards.fact: In 1453 Ottoman forces took Constantinople, ending the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire.
cards.detail: Sultan Mehmed II's army breached the great walls after a siege, aided by massive cannon. The city became the Ottoman capital. It is conventionally taken to mark the end of the Middle Ages and helped push scholars and trade routes westward — one spur for the Renaissance and for Europe's search for new sea routes.
cards.deploy: A clean marker for the end of the medieval order and the rise of the Ottomans as a Mediterranean great power.
cards.counter: Periodisation is a convenience: little changed overnight, and '1453 = end of the Middle Ages' is a tidy Eurocentric label.

quiz.q: What ended in 1453 with the fall of Constantinople?

cards.title: The French Revolution begins
cards.fact: On 14 July 1789 a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, igniting the French Revolution.
cards.detail: Fiscal crisis, a rigid estates system and high bread prices brought down the absolute monarchy. The Revolution produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man, a republic, the Terror, and ultimately Napoleon — spreading the language of citizenship, rights and nationalism across Europe.
cards.deploy: The hinge between divine-right monarchy and a modern politics of rights and citizenship.
cards.counter: Its ideals sat alongside the Terror and real exclusions (women, the enslaved in the colonies) — liberation and violence in one event.

quiz.q: The storming of the Bastille (14 July 1789) began which event?

cards.title: Humans land on the Moon
cards.fact: On 20 July 1969, Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon.
cards.detail: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface while Michael Collins orbited above. The feat was as much Cold War contest as science — a demonstration of capability against the Soviet Union after Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961).
cards.deploy: A peak example of what concentrated state funding and a clear goal can achieve in a few years.
cards.counter: It was driven by superpower rivalry as much as curiosity; crewed deep-space flight largely stalled once the point was made.

quiz.q: Which mission first landed humans on the Moon (1969)?

cards.title: The Hijra and year one of the Islamic calendar
cards.fact: 622 CE: Muhammad's migration (the Hijra) from Mecca to Medina marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar.
cards.detail: Facing persecution in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers relocated to Yathrib (Medina), where the first Muslim community and polity took shape. The Islamic lunar calendar (AH, 'after Hijra') counts from this year — not from Muhammad's birth or the first revelation.
cards.deploy: A reminder that the world's major calendars start from different events — dating itself encodes a worldview.
cards.counter: The year is firm, but precise days are reconstructed from later sources.

quiz.q: The Islamic calendar counts its years from…

cards.title: Sykes–Picot carves up the Middle East
cards.fact: 1916: the secret Sykes–Picot agreement split the Ottoman Middle East into British and French spheres.
cards.detail: During WWI, Britain and France (with Russian assent) secretly agreed how to divide the Ottoman Arab lands. The mandates and borders that followed — Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine — were drawn largely in European capitals, cutting across communities. The legacy still shapes Middle Eastern politics and grievances.
cards.deploy: Concrete evidence that many modern state borders were imposed from outside, not grown organically.
cards.counter: Later deals (San Remo, the mandate system) reshaped the lines; blaming all regional conflict on one 1916 map oversimplifies.

quiz.q: The 1916 Sykes–Picot agreement secretly divided…
choices: the Ottoman Middle East between Britain and France

cards.title: The founding of the People's Republic of China
cards.fact: 1 October 1949: Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China.
cards.detail: After decades of warlordism, Japanese invasion and civil war, the Communists under Mao defeated the Nationalists (who fled to Taiwan). The new state launched land reform and later the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution; from 1978 Deng Xiaoping's reforms opened the economy that made China a superpower.
cards.deploy: The starting point for understanding modern China's politics, economy and rise.
cards.counter: 1949 is a founding, not a steady state: Maoist and reform-era China differ so sharply they are almost different systems.

quiz.q: What was founded on 1 October 1949?

cards.title: The Year of Africa
cards.fact: 1960, the 'Year of Africa': 17 African countries gained independence from colonial rule.
cards.detail: In a single year a wave of mostly French and British colonies became sovereign states — Nigeria, Senegal, Mali, the Congo and others. Independence often came with borders inherited from the colonisers and economies built to export raw materials, shaping later challenges (including across the Sahel).
cards.deploy: Shows how recent decolonisation is — within living memory — and how colonial borders and economies outlast empire.
cards.counter: Formal independence didn't end external influence: Cold War rivalry, debt and 'Françafrique' ties kept shaping these states.

quiz.q: Why is 1960 called the 'Year of Africa'?

cards.title: The fall of the Berlin Wall
cards.fact: 9 November 1989: the Berlin Wall fell, symbolising the end of the Cold War division of Europe.
cards.detail: Mounting protest and a botched East German announcement sent crowds to the checkpoints; the guards stood aside. Within two years Germany reunified and the Soviet Union dissolved. It marked the collapse of the Eastern Bloc and, for a time, a sense that liberal democracy had 'won'.
cards.deploy: The emblematic end of the bipolar Cold War order and the start of a US-led 'unipolar moment'.
cards.counter: The 'end of history' optimism faded — authoritarian revival, great-power rivalry and the 2008 crisis complicated the triumphal story.

quiz.q: The fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) symbolised…
choices: the end of the Cold War division of Europe

cards.title: The prisoner's dilemma
cards.fact: Two people each acting in their own interest can both end up worse off than if they'd cooperated.
cards.detail: In the classic setup two suspects each do better by betraying the other no matter what the other does — so both betray, and both get a worse outcome than mutual silence. The individually rational move is collectively self-defeating. It models arms races, price wars, overfishing and climate inaction.
cards.deploy: The sharpest illustration that 'everyone acting rationally' need not produce a good outcome — a core case for coordination and rules.
cards.counter: Real life is rarely one-shot or anonymous; repetition, reputation and communication can rescue cooperation.

quiz.q: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, two self-interested players tend to…
choices: Both defect, ending up worse off

cards.title: Nash equilibrium
cards.fact: A Nash equilibrium is a situation where no player can do better by changing their move alone.
cards.detail: Named after John Nash, it is the resting point of a game: given what everyone else is doing, no one gains by deviating unilaterally. A game can have one, many, or no equilibria in pure strategies. Crucially, an equilibrium can be stable yet bad for everyone — mutual defection in the prisoner's dilemma is a Nash equilibrium.
cards.deploy: Lets you predict where strategic interactions settle — and show that a stable outcome isn't necessarily efficient or fair.
cards.counter: It assumes rational, payoff-maximising players who know the rules; real people misjudge, learn, and care about fairness.

quiz.q: At a Nash equilibrium…
choices: no player gains by changing strategy alone

cards.title: Repeated games and tit-for-tat
cards.fact: If a game is played again and again, cooperation can become rational — strategies like 'tit-for-tat' reward it and punish betrayal.
cards.detail: When players keep meeting, today's betrayal invites tomorrow's retaliation. In Axelrod's tournaments the simple 'tit-for-tat' rule — start nice, then copy the opponent's last move — did remarkably well. Repetition, reputation and a long 'shadow of the future' turn the prisoner's dilemma's logic around.
cards.deploy: Explains how cooperation emerges without a central enforcer — among firms, nations, even unrelated animals.
cards.counter: It needs a credible future: if the end is known and near, cooperation can unravel backwards from the final round.

quiz.q: Why can repetition sustain cooperation in a prisoner's dilemma?

cards.title: Valid vs true: the shape of an argument
cards.fact: An argument can be perfectly valid yet completely false — validity is about form, not facts.
cards.detail: An argument is valid if its conclusion must be true whenever its premises are — the logic holds regardless of content. It is sound only if it is valid AND its premises are actually true. 'All cats are robots; Felix is a cat; so Felix is a robot' is valid but unsound.
cards.deploy: Lets you separate two different complaints: 'your logic doesn't follow' vs 'your premise is false'.
cards.counter: Validity is necessary but cheap; in real debate the action is usually whether the premises are true, which logic alone can't settle.

quiz.q: An argument is valid when…
choices: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be too

cards.title: Modus ponens and modus tollens
cards.fact: Two reliable inference rules: affirm the 'if' (modus ponens) or deny the 'then' (modus tollens).
cards.detail: Modus ponens: from 'if P then Q' and 'P', conclude 'Q'. Modus tollens: from 'if P then Q' and 'not Q', conclude 'not P'. Both are valid forms — the backbone of everyday and mathematical reasoning. Popper's falsification is modus tollens: if a theory predicts Q and we observe not-Q, the theory fails.
cards.deploy: Names the moves so you can check whether a conclusion actually follows — and spot when someone only looks like they're using them.
cards.counter: Garbage in, garbage out: a valid form with a false 'if…then' premise still gives you nothing.

quiz.q: Modus tollens reasons from 'if P then Q' and 'not Q' to…

cards.title: Affirming the consequent
cards.fact: 'If P then Q; Q; therefore P' is a fallacy — a true consequence doesn't prove the cause.
cards.detail: Affirming the consequent confuses 'P implies Q' with 'Q implies P'. 'If it rained, the street is wet; the street is wet; so it rained' ignores sprinklers and hoses. It is one of the commonest reasoning errors — including in reading evidence: a result merely consistent with a theory doesn't confirm it.
cards.deploy: A precise label for a very common bad move — useful when someone treats 'consistent with' as 'proves'.
cards.counter: Such inferences can still raise the probability of P (that's Bayesian evidence) — they're just not deductively valid.

quiz.q: 'The street is wet, so it must have rained' commits which error?

cards.title: It's all bits
cards.fact: Everything in a computer — text, images, sound — is ultimately just numbers in binary (0s and 1s).
cards.detail: A bit is one on/off switch; eight bits make a byte. Numbers are written in base 2; text maps characters to numbers (ASCII/Unicode); images are grids of numbers for colour; sound is numbers sampled over time. The machine only ever shuffles patterns of bits — meaning is something we layer on top.
cards.deploy: Demystifies computers: no magic, just a very fast machine moving 0s and 1s under layers of convention.
cards.counter: 'It's all just bits' is true but unhelpful for understanding software — the interesting structure lives in the abstractions above.

quiz.q: At the lowest level, a computer stores text and images as…

cards.title: Big-O: how algorithms scale
cards.fact: Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's cost grows as the input gets bigger — not how fast it runs today.
cards.detail: An algorithm is a step-by-step recipe. Big-O captures scaling: O(n) doubles work when input doubles; O(n²) quadruples it; O(log n) barely grows. For large inputs a better Big-O beats a faster computer — an O(n log n) sort crushes an O(n²) one on a million items, whatever the hardware.
cards.deploy: Explains why 'use a better algorithm' often beats 'buy a faster computer' as data grows.
cards.counter: Big-O hides constant factors and real-world effects; for small inputs a 'worse' algorithm can be faster in practice.

quiz.q: Big-O notation describes an algorithm's…
choices: How its cost scales with input size

cards.title: The halting problem
cards.fact: Some problems are provably impossible for any computer: no program can decide, in general, whether another program will halt.
cards.detail: Alan Turing proved in 1936 that there is no general algorithm to decide whether an arbitrary program halts or loops forever — the halting problem. It set a hard limit on computation, echoing Gödel's incompleteness: formal systems and machines alike have questions they can't answer from the inside.
cards.deploy: Shows that 'undecidable' is a real, proven category — some questions have no algorithmic answer, however much power you throw at them.
cards.counter: Undecidability is about the general case; many specific instances are perfectly decidable, and approximations often suffice.

quiz.q: The halting problem shows that…
choices: No program can decide in general whether any program halts

cards.title: Law of large numbers (and the gambler's fallacy)
cards.fact: Averages settle down over many trials — but a fair coin has no memory, so 'due' outcomes are a fallacy.
cards.detail: The law of large numbers says the average of many independent trials converges to the true probability — flip a fair coin enough and heads approaches 50%. But each flip is independent: a run of tails doesn't make heads 'due'. Confusing the long-run average with short-run correction is the gambler's fallacy.
cards.deploy: Two lessons in one: trust large samples, and never expect chance to 'balance out' in the short run.
cards.counter: Convergence can be slow and assumes independence; with dependence or fat tails the average stays unstable far longer than intuition expects.

quiz.q: After five tails in a row, the chance of heads on a fair coin is…

cards.title: The central limit theorem
cards.fact: Add up many small independent effects and you tend to get a bell curve — the normal distribution.
cards.detail: The central limit theorem says sums or averages of many independent influences converge to a normal (Gaussian) shape, whatever the underlying distribution. That's why heights, measurement errors and sample averages cluster symmetrically around a mean — and why the bell curve and the standard deviation are everywhere in statistics.
cards.deploy: Explains why so many quantities are bell-shaped, and licenses much of standard statistics.
cards.counter: It fails when effects aren't independent or one factor dominates — then you get fat tails (power laws), where rare extremes are far commoner than the bell curve predicts.

quiz.q: The central limit theorem says sums of many independent effects tend toward a…

cards.title: Correlation isn't causation
cards.fact: Two things moving together may share a hidden common cause rather than one causing the other.
cards.detail: Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together — because both rise with summer heat, a confounder. To infer cause you need more: a plausible mechanism, controlled experiments (randomisation breaks confounding), or careful natural experiments. 'X correlates with Y' is the start of an investigation, not its conclusion.
cards.deploy: A precise check on causal claims from observational data — ask 'what's the confounder?' and 'was it randomised?'
cards.counter: Overused as a thought-stopper: correlation is real evidence, and good design (instrumental variables, natural experiments) can infer causation without a lab.

quiz.q: Ice-cream sales correlate with drownings mainly because…
choices: Both rise with summer heat (a confounder)

cards.title: Good names are the cheapest documentation
cards.fact: Code is read far more often than it's written, so clear names are the highest-leverage documentation there is.
cards.detail: A variable called daysSinceLastLogin needs no comment; d needs a paragraph. Good names state intent — what something is or does — so the next reader (often you, months later) doesn't have to reverse-engineer it. Renaming for clarity is one of the safest, most valuable edits you can make.
cards.deploy: The simplest lever for maintainable software: spend the extra seconds naming things well.
cards.counter: Names can't carry everything; over-long or 'clever' names hurt as much as cryptic ones — the goal is clarity, not length.

quiz.q: Clear names matter most because code is…
choices: Read far more often than it's written

cards.title: Don't repeat yourself (DRY)
cards.fact: Every piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place in the code.
cards.detail: When the same logic is copied in several spots, changing it means finding every copy — and missing one creates bugs. DRY says capture it once (a function, a constant, a single source of truth) so a change happens in exactly one place. It's about duplicated knowledge, not just identical text.
cards.deploy: Explains why copy-paste programming rots: each duplicate is a future inconsistency waiting to happen.
cards.counter: Premature DRY is its own trap — forcing unlike things to share code creates tangled coupling. A little duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

quiz.q: DRY is mainly about avoiding duplication of…

cards.title: Code is for humans: manage complexity
cards.fact: The hard part of programming isn't writing code — it's keeping complexity low enough to keep changing it.
cards.detail: As software grows the limit isn't the computer but the human: how much you can hold in your head. Small functions, clear boundaries between parts, and hiding details behind simple surfaces keep local changes local. The aim is code you can safely modify without understanding all of it at once.
cards.deploy: Reframes 'good code' as 'code that's cheap to change' — the real cost is maintenance, not the first draft.
cards.counter: Abstraction has a price: too many layers can obscure as much as sprawl. The skill is matching structure to the problem, not maximising either.

quiz.q: As software grows, the main constraint is…
choices: Human ability to understand and change it

cards.title: Octopuses have three hearts
cards.fact: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
cards.detail: Two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills; one systemic heart sends it to the body. The blood carries oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin (blue) rather than iron-based haemoglobin (red), which works better in cold, low-oxygen water.
cards.deploy: A vivid example that evolution finds many independent solutions to the same problem (oxygen transport) — there is rarely one 'right' design.
cards.counter: It's a trade-off, not strictly 'better': haemocyanin carries less oxygen than haemoglobin at warm temperatures.

quiz.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
An octopus's blue blood carries oxygen using…

cards.title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
cards.fact: Venus takes longer to spin once than to orbit the Sun.
cards.detail: Venus rotates once every ~243 Earth days but orbits the Sun every ~225 Earth days — and it spins backwards (retrograde). So by the sidereal definition, its 'day' outlasts its 'year'.
cards.deploy: Everyday intuitions ('a day is shorter than a year') are local conventions, not universal truths.
cards.counter: It depends on the definition: a solar day on Venus (sunrise to sunrise) is ~117 Earth days, because the retrograde spin and orbit partly cancel.

cards.title: The Year Without a Summer (1816)
cards.fact: In 1816 a volcano half a world away caused snow in June and famine across the Northern Hemisphere.
cards.detail: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia — the largest in recorded history — threw sulfate aerosols into the stratosphere, dimming the sun and crashing temperatures. Crops failed across Europe and North America. The gloom of that summer also gave us Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein'.
cards.deploy: A single physical event can cascade into global social, economic and even cultural effects.
cards.counter: Attribution is partly confounded by an overlapping solar minimum (the Dalton Minimum); the volcano was the main driver but not the only one.

cards.title: Honey effectively never spoils
cards.fact: Sealed honey can stay edible for thousands of years — pots found in Egyptian tombs were still good.
cards.detail: Honey's very low water content, acidity, and the trace hydrogen peroxide released by an enzyme (glucose oxidase) make it hostile to microbes. Kept sealed and dry, it lasts indefinitely.
cards.deploy: Preservation can be a property of chemistry, not refrigeration — a clean counterexample to 'all food rots'.
cards.counter: Only while sealed: add water (or contamination) and honey will ferment. Crystallisation is normal and reversible, not spoilage.

cards.title: Some infinities are bigger than others
cards.fact: There are strictly more real numbers than whole numbers — infinity comes in different sizes.
cards.detail: Cantor's diagonal argument (1891) shows you can't list all real numbers even with an infinite list: given any list, you can build a real number missing from it. So the reals are 'uncountable' and outnumber the (countable) integers.
cards.deploy: Stops loose appeals to infinity: 'infinite' does not mean 'all the same' or 'anything goes'.
cards.counter: Whether there's a size strictly between the integers and the reals (the Continuum Hypothesis) is provably undecidable in standard set theory (Gödel 1940, Cohen 1963).

quiz.q: Cantor's diagonal argument shows the real numbers are…
choices: The same size as the integers

quiz.q: Which set is the 'bigger', uncountable infinity?

cards.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
cards.fact: Any consistent maths system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it can never prove.
cards.detail: Gödel (1931) showed such a system can't be both complete and consistent, and can't prove its own consistency from within. Truth outruns provability.
cards.deploy: A hard limit on formal systems — useful against claims that 'anything true can, in principle, be proven'.
cards.counter: Routinely overstated. It applies to specific formal systems, not to 'all reasoning'; it does not imply 'nothing is knowable' or license mysticism.

media.caption: Bayes' theorem. Read the bar '|' as 'given'. It updates the chance of A once you've seen B — and P(A), the base rate, never drops out, which is exactly what the fallacy forgets.

cards.title: The base-rate fallacy
cards.fact: A 99%-accurate test for a rare disease still produces mostly false positives.
cards.detail: If a disease affects 1 in 1,000 and a test is 99% accurate, a positive result is far more likely to be a false alarm than a real case, because there are so many more healthy people to misclassify. The prior (base rate) dominates.
cards.deploy: Demand the base rate before accepting 'the test/study says X'. Accuracy figures alone can badly mislead.
cards.counter: Bayesian reasoning needs a defensible prior; with a bad prior you just get confidently wrong posteriors.

quiz.q: For a rare condition, a positive result on a highly accurate test is…

cards.title: Simpson's paradox
cards.fact: A trend can hold in every subgroup yet reverse when the groups are combined.
cards.detail: In Berkeley's 1973 graduate admissions, men appeared admitted at higher rates overall, yet within most departments women were admitted at equal-or-higher rates — women applied more to competitive departments. Aggregation flipped the picture.
cards.deploy: Aggregate numbers can mislead — always ask whether a confounder is hiding inside the average.
cards.counter: Which view is 'correct' isn't a rule of thumb; it depends on the underlying causal structure, which the data alone can't settle.

cards.title: Entropy and the arrow of time
cards.fact: In an isolated system, entropy never decreases — which is why time has a direction.
cards.detail: The second law of thermodynamics: usable energy disperses; ordered states drift toward disorder. It's why heat flows hot→cold and why a smashed cup never reassembles.
cards.deploy: Rules out perpetual-motion and 'free lunch' schemes — there's always a cost paid somewhere.
cards.counter: Local order can increase (life, fridges, crystals) as long as total entropy rises — a frequent misuse is citing the second law against evolution.

cards.title: The speed of light is the same for everyone
cards.fact: Light travels at the same speed for all observers, no matter how they move.
cards.detail: Einstein's 1905 special relativity takes this as a postulate. The consequences are strange but measured: moving clocks run slow (time dilation), moving lengths contract, and simultaneity is relative.
cards.deploy: Shows 'common sense' about absolute time and simultaneity is simply wrong — verified by GPS, particle accelerators, atomic clocks.
cards.counter: Newtonian mechanics remains an excellent approximation at everyday speeds; relativity refines it, it doesn't make it 'useless'.

media.caption: The more precisely you fix position (Δx), the less precisely momentum (Δp) is fixed.

cards.title: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
cards.fact: You cannot know a particle's exact position and momentum at the same time.
cards.detail: The product of the uncertainties in position and momentum has a hard floor (Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2). It's a feature of nature, not a limit of our instruments.
cards.deploy: There are fundamental, not merely practical, limits to measurement.
cards.counter: Frequently abused by analogy ('the observer changes everything') in social or business arguments where it simply doesn't apply.

cards.title: We can still see the Big Bang's afterglow
cards.fact: The whole sky glows faintly at ~2.7 K — leftover heat from the early universe.
cards.detail: Penzias and Wilson detected the cosmic microwave background in 1964 (published 1965), a relic of when the universe cooled enough for light to travel freely ~380,000 years after the Big Bang. It's some of the strongest evidence for the hot Big Bang model.
cards.deploy: The Big Bang is evidence-backed, not mere speculation — we literally observe its relic radiation.
cards.counter: 'Big Bang' describes the expansion from a hot, dense state — it does not claim to explain the ultimate origin or 'what banged'.

cards.title: Gutenberg's printing press (~1440)
cards.fact: Cheap printed books in the 1400s helped trigger the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.
cards.detail: Movable-type printing in Europe (~1440) collapsed the cost of copying text. Literacy spread, ideas travelled faster than authorities could suppress them, and standardised knowledge accumulated.
cards.deploy: Information technology reshapes who holds power — a historical anchor for arguments about the printing press / internet / AI.
cards.counter: Printing predates Gutenberg in East Asia (Bi Sheng's movable type ~1040, Korean metal type earlier). His contribution was the European system and its economics, not the raw idea.

cards.title: The Black Death (1347–1351)
cards.fact: A plague that killed a third or more of Europe also raised the wages of those who survived.
cards.detail: With labour suddenly scarce, surviving workers could demand more, accelerating the decline of serfdom in parts of Western Europe. Catastrophe restructured the economy.
cards.deploy: Shocks can shift the balance of power between labour and capital — scarcity changes bargaining position.
cards.counter: The 'wages rose' story varies sharply by region and institutions; in places elites tightened controls instead. Single mechanisms oversimplify.

cards.title: The Peace of Westphalia (1648)
cards.fact: The 1648 treaties ending the Thirty Years' War are often called the birth of the sovereign state.
cards.detail: They're cited as the origin of 'Westphalian sovereignty' — the principle that states are supreme within their own borders and don't answer to outside authority.
cards.deploy: A foundational reference for debates about national sovereignty vs international intervention.
cards.counter: Historians (e.g. Andreas Osiander) argue the 'Westphalian myth' is a 19th-century back-projection; the treaties didn't actually establish modern sovereignty as commonly claimed.

cards.title: The Thucydides Trap
cards.fact: When a rising power threatens a ruling one, the result is often war.
cards.detail: Graham Allison studied 16 cases over 500 years and found war in 12. Named after Thucydides' line that it was the rise of Athens, and the fear it caused in Sparta, that made war inevitable. Applied today to the US and China.
cards.deploy: A structured frame for great-power-rivalry arguments — names the mechanism (fear of a shifting balance).
cards.counter: The case selection and what counts as a 'rise' or 'war' are contested; 'often' is not 'inevitable', and 4 of 16 avoided war.

cards.title: Chokepoint: the Strait of Hormuz
cards.fact: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through one narrow strait.
cards.detail: About 20–21 million barrels a day move through the Strait of Hormuz between the Persian Gulf and open ocean — a single point of geographic leverage.
cards.deploy: Physical geography concentrates strategic power — concrete grounding for arguments about energy security.
cards.counter: Shares and volumes shift; new pipelines and changing demand steadily reduce any one chokepoint's leverage.

cards.title: Mackinder's Heartland theory (1904)
cards.fact: Whoever controls the Eurasian 'Heartland' could dominate the world — a classic land-power doctrine.
cards.detail: Halford Mackinder argued that control of inner Eurasia (the 'World-Island') was the key to global power, because it was beyond the reach of sea power.
cards.deploy: The founding lens of geopolitical 'land power vs sea power' thinking — still echoed in analyses of Russia and Central Asia.
cards.counter: Airpower, nuclear weapons, and globalised trade undercut pure land-centric determinism; geography constrains but doesn't dictate.

cards.title: The demographic transition
cards.fact: As countries develop, they shift from high birth-and-death rates to low — then they age.
cards.detail: Falling child mortality and development first cause a population boom, then birth rates fall and the population stabilises and greys, raising the ratio of retirees to workers.
cards.deploy: Explains why growth slows and why ageing (China, Japan, Europe) reshapes economies and pensions.
cards.counter: Trajectories vary widely; immigration, policy, and culture can speed up, slow down, or reverse parts of the transition.

cards.title: Natural selection
cards.fact: Heritable variation plus differential survival produces design without a designer.
cards.detail: Darwin (1859): organisms vary, some variations are inherited, and those that aid survival and reproduction become more common over generations — yielding apparent design.
cards.deploy: Complexity can arise from blind, cumulative processes — the canonical answer to 'it looks designed, so it was designed'.
cards.counter: Selection is one mechanism among several. Genetic drift, gene flow, and sheer contingency also shape evolution; not every trait is an adaptation.

quiz.q: Natural selection requires variation that is…

cards.title: You're about half bacteria (by cell count)
cards.fact: Your body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells — about 1:1, not the old '10:1'.
cards.detail: A 2016 re-estimate put it near 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells. The widely-repeated '10 times more bacteria than your own cells' was never well-founded.
cards.deploy: Doubles as a fact and a myth-correction — a clean way to show how a 'known' figure can be wrong.
cards.counter: These are estimates with wide ranges and they vary person to person; function matters more than raw counts.

cards.title: CRISPR: programmable gene editing
cards.fact: Since 2012 we've been able to cut and edit DNA at a chosen spot, cheaply and precisely.
cards.detail: Doudna and Charpentier showed the bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 system can be guided by a custom RNA to cut DNA wherever you point it (Nobel Prize 2020). It transformed biotech almost overnight.
cards.deploy: Cheap, precise editing changes every debate about medicine, agriculture, and 'designer' organisms.
cards.counter: Off-target edits and the ethics of heritable (germline) changes remain serious, unresolved caveats.

cards.title: Wolves reshaped Yellowstone
cards.fact: Reintroducing wolves in 1995 rippled all the way down to the rivers.
cards.detail: With wolves back, elk grazed differently, letting willow and aspen recover, which helped beavers and stabilised some streambanks — a 'trophic cascade' from a top predator.
cards.deploy: Top predators have outsized, system-wide effects — a memorable case that removing one species isn't a local change.
cards.counter: The popular 'wolves changed the rivers' story is partly overstated; recovery had multiple drivers and the magnitude is debated.

cards.title: Planetary boundaries
cards.fact: Scientists have mapped nine limits for a stable planet — and we've crossed several.
cards.detail: The framework defines a 'safe operating space' across climate, biodiversity, the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, freshwater, land use, and more. A 2023 update found six of nine boundaries transgressed.
cards.deploy: Moves environmental debate from 'climate only' to a systems view of multiple, interacting limits.
cards.counter: The specific boundary values carry real uncertainty, and some boundaries are global while others are really regional — the numbers are estimates, not constants.

cards.title: Half the nitrogen in you came from one factory process
cards.fact: The Haber-Bosch process (1909) pulls nitrogen from the air to make fertiliser — and now feeds roughly half the world.
cards.detail: Before it, crop yields were capped by natural nitrogen. Synthetic ammonia broke that ceiling; a large share of the nitrogen atoms in your body passed through this industrial reaction.
cards.deploy: One chemical process underpins modern food security — a striking dependency to put on the table.
cards.counter: It's double-edged: the same nitrogen runoff drives algal blooms, dead zones, and potent nitrous-oxide emissions.

cards.title: Reinforcing vs balancing feedback
cards.fact: Two loop types explain most system behaviour: one amplifies, one stabilises.
cards.detail: Reinforcing (positive) loops compound — interest, viral spread, arms races. Balancing (negative) loops push back toward a target — a thermostat, hunger, market correction.
cards.deploy: Lets you name why something grows explosively or stays stubbornly stable instead of hand-waving.
cards.counter: Real systems chain many loops with delays; reading off a single loop usually misleads.

cards.title: The tragedy of the commons — and its rebuttal
cards.fact: Shared resources get overused when each user pockets the gain but shares the cost — yet communities often solve this without the state or markets.
cards.detail: Hardin (1968) argued a shared pasture is doomed to overgrazing. Elinor Ostrom (Nobel 2009) then documented many real communities that govern shared fisheries, forests and irrigation sustainably through their own rules.
cards.deploy: Carries its own counter-argument: useful whether you're arguing for regulation OR for local self-governance.
cards.counter: Hardin overgeneralised from a model; Ostrom showed the 'tragedy' is not inevitable when users can communicate and make binding rules.

cards.title: Heavy tails: when the average lies
cards.fact: Wealth, city sizes, and word frequencies follow heavy-tailed distributions where a few cases dominate.
cards.detail: In a power-law-like distribution, the 'typical' value and the average can be wildly different — think the 80/20 rule. A handful of extreme cases carry most of the total.
cards.deploy: Warns against reasoning from the mean in unequal systems — 'average income' or 'average user' can be meaningless.
cards.counter: True power laws are statistically hard to distinguish from lognormal distributions, and the label is often slapped on data that doesn't fit it.

cards.title: Comparative advantage
cards.fact: Two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at making everything.

layers.body: Say one country is better at making both wine and cloth. It still pays both sides to specialise and trade. What matters isn't who's better in absolute terms, but who gives up the least to make a thing — its opportunity cost.

David Ricardo set this out in 1817. If each country makes the good it sacrifices least to produce, and trades for the rest, total output rises and both can end up with more than they could alone. It is the textbook case for free trade.

The clean result leans on strong assumptions: full employment, resources that move easily between industries, and no account of who wins or loses inside a country. In the real world trade can grow the pie while specific workers and regions are hollowed out — a theory about totals, not about distribution.

cards.detail: Ricardo (1817): what matters is opportunity cost, not absolute skill. Each side specialises where it gives up the least, and total output rises. It's the core case for trade.
cards.deploy: The standard answer to 'they can make it cheaper, so trade hurts us' — gains come from specialisation, not from winning at everything.
cards.counter: The clean result assumes full employment, mobile resources, and ignores distribution: trade can raise the total while leaving specific workers and regions worse off.

quiz.q: Comparative advantage says gains from trade come from differences in…
A country should specialise where it has the lowest…

cards.title: Externalities
cards.fact: When a cost or benefit lands on third parties, the market price gets it wrong.
cards.detail: Pollution is the classic case: a factory's price doesn't include the harm downstream. Pigou (1920) proposed taxing the activity to make the price tell the truth.
cards.deploy: Justifies carbon taxes, congestion charges, and the like: prices need correcting when costs spill over.
cards.counter: Coase (1960) showed that with clear property rights and low bargaining costs, private parties can fix externalities without taxes — the right remedy depends on the situation.

cards.title: Loss aversion
cards.fact: Losing $100 hurts about twice as much as gaining $100 feels good.
cards.detail: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory (1979) showed people don't weigh outcomes by final wealth but by gains and losses from a reference point — and losses loom larger. It helped found behavioural economics.
cards.deploy: Undercuts the assumption that people are cool rational maximisers — framing a choice as a loss vs a gain changes behaviour.
cards.counter: The exact 2:1 ratio varies by context and there's ongoing replication debate; it's a robust tendency, not a fixed constant.

cards.title: Hume's is–ought gap
cards.fact: You can't logically derive what ought to be purely from what is.
cards.detail: Hume (1739) noticed writers slide from describing facts ('is') to prescribing duties ('ought') without justifying the jump. Facts alone don't entail values.
cards.deploy: A precision tool for spotting when an opponent smuggles a value claim in under cover of 'the science says'.
cards.counter: Some philosophers (ethical naturalists) argue the gap can be bridged; it's a powerful warning, not a settled proof that values float free of facts.

cards.title: Falsifiability
cards.fact: A claim that nothing could ever disprove isn't really scientific.
cards.detail: Popper argued the mark of a scientific theory is that it sticks its neck out — it forbids certain observations, so it could be proven wrong. 'What would change your mind?' is the key question.
cards.deploy: A sharp test against unfalsifiable claims ('it's true, you just can't see the evidence').
cards.counter: Kuhn and Lakatos showed real science doesn't work by naive falsification — a failed prediction is often blamed on auxiliary assumptions, not the core theory.

quiz.q: For Popper, a scientific theory must be…
By Popper's criterion, which claim is LEAST scientific (unfalsifiable)?
choices: Heavy objects fall at g in a vacuum
Whatever happens was meant to be
Water boils at 100°C at sea level

cards.title: Rawls's veil of ignorance
cards.fact: To find fair rules, choose them not knowing who you'll be in the society.
cards.detail: Rawls (1971): behind a 'veil' that hides your wealth, talents, race and class, you'd pick principles that protect everyone — because you might end up at the bottom.
cards.deploy: A portable fairness test for any institution or policy: would you accept it not knowing your place in it?
cards.counter: Nozick and others reject the setup: why assume people behind the veil would be so risk-averse (favouring the worst-off) rather than gambling on the average?

cards.title: The median voter theorem
cards.fact: In a simple two-way majority vote, the middle voter decides — so parties drift to the centre.
cards.detail: If opinion lines up on one axis and the winner needs a majority, the option preferred by the median voter beats all others. Candidates converge toward that voter to win.
cards.deploy: Explains why rival parties can end up sounding alike — a clean model for centrist convergence.
cards.counter: It assumes one dimension, two options, and full turnout. Primaries, multidimensional issues, and abstention routinely break it.

cards.title: Duverger's law
cards.fact: Winner-take-all elections tend to produce two big parties; proportional systems produce many.
cards.detail: Under first-past-the-post, votes for small parties are 'wasted', so voters and donors consolidate around two contenders. Proportional representation rewards smaller parties, so more survive.
cards.deploy: Shows that party systems are shaped by the voting rules, not just by the electorate's views — institutions matter.
cards.counter: It's a tendency, not an iron law: the UK and India sustain strong regional/third parties under the same rules.

cards.title: The collective action problem
cards.fact: Even when everyone would benefit, large groups often fail to act — because each person can free-ride.
cards.detail: Olson (1965): if you'll get the benefit whether or not you contribute, the rational move is to let others do the work. So big diffuse groups under-organise while small concentrated interests punch above their weight.
cards.deploy: Explains why concentrated lobbies beat diffuse majorities, and why obvious public goods get under-provided.
cards.counter: Selective incentives, social pressure, leadership, and repeated interaction (Ostrom) routinely overcome free-riding — it's a hurdle, not a wall.

cards.title: What economics is about
cards.fact: Economics starts from one awkward fact: we have unlimited wants and limited means.

layers.body: Because you can't have everything, every choice means giving something up. Economics studies how people, firms and societies make those trade-offs — what gets produced, how, and for whom.

The cost of any choice is the best thing you gave up to get it: its opportunity cost. An hour studying is an hour not earning; money for one programme is money not spent on another. Thinking in opportunity costs is the discipline's signature move.

How far this 'scarcity and choice' frame should reach is itself disputed. Critics argue it quietly assumes wants are fixed and that everything trades off against everything, while sidelining power, history and institutions. It's a useful lens on economic life, not the whole of it.

cards.detail: Because you can't have everything, every choice means giving something up. Economics studies how people and societies handle those trade-offs — and the cost of any choice is the best alternative you gave up (its opportunity cost).
cards.deploy: Reframes almost any policy fight as 'what are we giving up?' rather than just 'is this nice?'.
cards.counter: The scarcity frame can hide questions of power and distribution — who decides what's scarce, and for whom.

quiz.q: The opportunity cost of a choice is…
choices: The best alternative you gave up

quiz.q: Economics begins from the problem of…

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.fact: In the basic model, price isn't set by cost or fairness — it's where supply meets demand.

layers.body: When something gets pricier, people tend to want less of it and producers want to make more. The price moves until the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. That balance point is the market 'equilibrium'.

Shift either side and the price moves: a frost cuts the coffee supply and prices rise; a fad lifts demand and prices rise too. Two simple curves explain a huge range of everyday price moves — which is why it's the first thing taught.

The neat diagram assumes many small buyers and sellers, good information, and no one big enough to set prices. Real markets have monopolies, advertising, habit, and 'sticky' wages and rents that don't budge. Supply and demand is a starting model, not a law of nature.

cards.detail: When price rises, buyers want less and sellers offer more; the price settles where the two meet. It's a powerful starting model — but it assumes competition, good information and flexible prices that real markets often lack.
cards.deploy: Explains why price caps tend to cause shortages and why some subsidies just push prices up.
cards.counter: Perfect competition is rare; with market power, information gaps or sticky prices the simple model can mislead.

quiz.q: In the basic model, the market price settles where…

cards.title: What GDP measures
cards.fact: GDP measures the money value of what a country produces — and quietly leaves a lot out.

layers.body: Gross Domestic Product adds up the market value of all the goods and services a country makes in a year. It's the headline number for 'the size of the economy' and whether it's growing.

Because it counts only what's bought and sold, GDP ignores unpaid care and housework, says nothing about who gets the income, and even counts cleaning up pollution as a gain. Simon Kuznets, who helped build it in the 1930s, warned it should never be mistaken for national wellbeing.

Whether to chase GDP growth is one of economics' sharpest fault lines. Some argue growth lifts living standards and funds everything else; ecological and feminist economists argue it counts the wrong things and can't continue forever on a finite planet. The proposed alternatives — the Human Development Index, 'doughnut' economics, wellbeing budgets — are contested too.

cards.detail: GDP totals the market value of a country's output. It misses unpaid work, ignores distribution, and treats some harms as gains — which is why 'growth' is one of economics' biggest arguments.
cards.deploy: Cuts through 'the economy grew, so we're better off' — ask what the number counts and what it omits.
cards.counter: For all its flaws, GDP tracks real things — jobs, output, tax revenue — and no rival measure has cleanly replaced it.

quiz.q: GDP does NOT directly count…

cards.title: Why 'political economy'?
cards.fact: Before it was 'economics', it was 'political economy' — and the politics never really left.

layers.body: For Smith, Ricardo and Marx the subject was 'political economy': how wealth is produced and, above all, how it's divided between landlords, workers and owners. Economics and power were studied together.

Around 1900 the field renamed itself 'economics' and modelled itself on physics — equilibrium, optimisation, mathematics. Questions of class and power moved to the margins. 'Political economy' survived as the name for approaches that put them back at the centre.

Is economics a neutral, technical science or an inescapably political one? Mainstream economists stress method and evidence; critics argue every model embeds a view of human nature and a politics of distribution. The very word you choose — 'economics' or 'political economy' — already takes a side.

cards.detail: The classical writers studied 'political economy' — wealth and its distribution between classes. Around 1900 the field rebranded as 'economics' on the model of physics, pushing power to the margins; 'political economy' names the traditions that keep it central.
cards.deploy: Reminds an opponent that 'just the economics' is rarely just the economics.
cards.counter: Naming the politics doesn't settle the facts — efficiency and distribution can still be studied with evidence.

cards.title: The rival schools
cards.fact: There is no single 'economics' — there are rival schools that disagree about how the economy works.

layers.body: Ask 'what causes unemployment?' or 'what is money?' and the answer depends on the tradition: classical, Marxian, neoclassical, Keynesian, monetarist, Austrian, behavioural, ecological. Each has its own assumptions and its own heroes.

Classical (Smith, Ricardo) on growth and value; Marxian on class and exploitation; neoclassical on rational choice and equilibrium; Keynesian on demand and slumps; monetarist (Friedman) on the money supply; Austrian (Hayek) on prices as information; behavioural on how real people actually decide; ecological on the economy nested inside the biosphere.

Mainstream teaching is dominated by the neoclassical–Keynesian synthesis, and students often meet it simply as 'economics'. Pluralist movements argue this narrows the imagination, and that the 2008 crisis exposed the cost of teaching one paradigm as settled truth.

cards.detail: Economics is plural: classical, Marxian, neoclassical, Keynesian, monetarist, Austrian, behavioural and ecological schools give different answers to the same questions. The mainstream is one paradigm among several, not the last word.
cards.deploy: Whenever someone says 'economists agree', ask which economists — the field is plural.
cards.counter: Pluralism can tip into 'anything goes'; some claims really are better supported by the evidence than others.

cards.title: Adam Smith and the invisible hand
cards.fact: Smith argued a butcher feeds you not from kindness but from self-interest — and somehow it works.

layers.body: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Smith argued that people pursuing their own gain, guided 'as if by an invisible hand', can produce outcomes that benefit everyone. Markets coordinate millions of strangers without anyone planning the whole.

Smith's deeper mechanism was the division of labour — splitting work into specialised tasks multiplies output enormously — and free exchange lets that specialisation spread. He is claimed as the founder of free-market economics.

Smith is routinely flattened into a cheerleader for greed. In fact the phrase 'invisible hand' appears once in the book; his earlier Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) roots society in sympathy, not selfishness. He distrusted merchants, warned they conspire against the public, and backed some state action. Left and right both quote him selectively.

cards.detail: Smith (1776) argued self-interested exchange, coordinated 'as if by an invisible hand', can benefit all, powered by the division of labour. But he also rooted society in sympathy and distrusted merchants — he's far more nuanced than the caricature.
cards.deploy: Useful against caricatures of 'capitalism = greed is good' — even Smith didn't say that.
cards.counter: Smith still defended self-interest and markets as broadly benign — he isn't the proto-socialist some make him either.

quiz.q: Smith's 'invisible hand' is the idea that…

cards.title: The division of labour
cards.fact: Smith watched a pin factory and saw the secret of modern wealth: split the job up.

layers.body: One worker doing every step might make a handful of pins a day. Split the work into around eighteen specialised steps and a small team makes tens of thousands. Specialisation, not harder effort, is what explodes output.

Division of labour raises skill, saves time switching tasks, and invites machinery. Smith made it the foundation of growth — but he also warned that a worker repeating one motion all day could become 'as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become'.

Marx pushed that worry much further, arguing extreme division of labour 'alienates' workers from their work, each other and themselves. The same mechanism that creates wealth can deskill and dull the people doing it — efficiency and human flourishing can pull apart.

cards.detail: Splitting work into specialised steps multiplies output — Smith's pin factory is the classic example. But he and later Marx warned it can also deskill and alienate the worker.
cards.deploy: Explains assembly lines, supply chains and outsourcing — and their human downside.
cards.counter: Specialisation also lifted billions out of subsistence; the gains are real, not just the costs.

cards.title: Ricardo and the logic machine
cards.fact: David Ricardo turned economics into a machine of pure logic — and reached unsettling conclusions.

layers.body: A stockbroker turned theorist, Ricardo (1817) built spare models from a few assumptions and followed them ruthlessly. He gave us comparative advantage, the theory of rent, and a labour-based theory of value.

His theory of rent: as population grows, worse land gets farmed, so rents rise and landlords gain at everyone else's expense — an early model of distribution as a conflict between classes. And he argued a good's value comes mainly from the labour needed to produce it.

Ricardo's labour theory of value was picked up by Marx, then dropped by the mainstream after the 1870s 'marginal revolution', which located value in usefulness at the margin instead. Whether value is 'really' about labour or about subjective utility is an old fault line that still shapes which economics you're taught.

cards.detail: Ricardo built ruthless logical models: comparative advantage, the theory of rent (landlords gain as population grows), and a labour theory of value later taken up by Marx and dropped by the mainstream.
cards.deploy: Shows distribution-as-class-conflict has deep roots inside classical economics, not just in Marx.
cards.counter: The labour theory of value faces hard problems (capital, time, skill) that marginalism was designed to solve.

cards.title: Where does value come from?
cards.fact: Is a thing valuable because of the work in it, or because of how much you want it?

layers.body: The classical economists (Smith, Ricardo) and then Marx held a labour theory of value: a good's value reflects the socially necessary labour time to produce it. A diamond is dear because it's hard to find and cut, not just because it sparkles.

Marx used it to argue that workers produce more value than they're paid; the gap — 'surplus value' — becomes profit and the source of capital. On this view profit isn't a reward for risk but a claim on others' labour.

From the 1870s the marginalists (Jevons, Menger, Walras) replaced it: value comes from the usefulness of the last unit to a buyer, set by supply and demand. This is now textbook orthodoxy. Heterodox and Marxian economists keep the labour theory alive, arguing marginalism hides the social relations behind prices. It's a choice of framework, not a closed case.

cards.detail: Classical economists and Marx located value in labour; marginalists from the 1870s relocated it in usefulness at the margin. The mainstream took the second path — but the first still frames profit as extraction rather than reward.
cards.deploy: Lets you locate an argument: profit-as-reward (marginalist) vs profit-as-extraction (Marxian).
cards.counter: Marginalism resolved real puzzles — like why water is cheap and diamonds dear — that the labour theory struggled with.

cards.title: The marginal revolution (1870s)
cards.fact: In the 1870s economics quietly changed its mind about what value even is.

layers.body: Within a few years Jevons in England, Menger in Austria and Walras in Switzerland independently argued that value comes from marginal utility — the usefulness of one more unit — not from labour. This 'marginal revolution' founded neoclassical economics.

It rebuilt the subject around individuals maximising satisfaction subject to constraints, expressed in calculus. Water is cheap because the last glass is barely needed; diamonds are dear because each is highly wanted at the margin. Markets became a story about optimising agents meeting in equilibrium.

The change was intellectual and arguably political: it moved economics away from class and distribution — the classical and Marxian focus — toward individual choice and efficiency, where the system tends to a harmonious balance. Critics say this 'depoliticised' the field; defenders say it made it rigorous and testable.

cards.detail: Around 1871–1874, Jevons, Menger and Walras relocated value in marginal utility, founding neoclassical economics and shifting the field from class and distribution toward individual optimisation and equilibrium.
cards.deploy: Explains why mainstream economics talks about utility and equilibrium rather than class.
cards.counter: The marginalist tools genuinely unified price theory and remain the workhorse of applied economics.

cards.title: Marx's Capital
cards.fact: Marx didn't just dislike capitalism — he tried to reverse-engineer its hidden machinery.

layers.body: In Das Kapital (volume 1, 1867) Marx set out to explain how capitalism actually works. Workers sell their labour for a wage but produce more value than they're paid; that 'surplus value' becomes profit and is reinvested as ever-growing capital.

Competition forces owners to accumulate, mechanise and cut costs, which Marx argued tends to push down the rate of profit, throw workers out of jobs, and produce recurring crises of overproduction. Capitalism, on his account, is dynamic and revolutionary but unstable and prone to concentration.

Marx's specific predictions — falling profit rates, ever-deepening worker poverty, inevitable collapse — haven't played out cleanly; living standards rose and the labour theory of value he relied on is rejected by the mainstream. Yet his analysis of inequality, crises, monopoly and capital's restlessness keeps being rediscovered, including after 2008. Influential as critique, contested as prophecy.

cards.detail: Marx (1867) argued workers produce more value than their wage ('surplus value'), the source of profit and capital; competition drives accumulation, crises and concentration. His critique outlived his failed predictions.
cards.deploy: A structured frame for arguments about exploitation, inequality and recurring financial crises.
cards.counter: Where Marxist regimes took power, central planning produced its own shortages and repression — the cure has a grim record too.

quiz.q: For Marx, profit ('surplus value') comes from…
choices: Value workers produce above their wage

cards.title: Historical materialism
cards.fact: Marx's big bet: to understand history, follow how people make their living.

layers.body: Historical materialism is the idea that a society's economic base — how it produces and who owns what — shapes its politics, law, religion and ideas more than the other way round. Change how a society makes its living and the rest eventually shifts.

On this view history moves through stages — feudalism, capitalism, and Marx hoped socialism — as new productive forces strain against old ownership arrangements until the tensions break. Ideas and institutions are partly 'superstructure' resting on that economic base.

Critics call it economic determinism — ideas, religion and politics plainly shape economies too (Max Weber argued Protestant culture helped birth capitalism). Most historians now reject any single master key to history. But 'follow the material interests' remains a powerful analytical habit, even for non-Marxists.

cards.detail: Historical materialism holds that the economic base shapes a society's politics and ideas, and that history advances as productive forces outgrow old ownership arrangements. Powerful as a habit of analysis, contested as a law of history.
cards.deploy: Prompts the sharp question: 'whose material interests does this idea serve?'.
cards.counter: Culture, religion and ideas have driven huge changes no economic base predicted.

cards.title: Keynes and the stuck economy
cards.fact: Keynes argued a market economy can get stuck in a slump — and just sit there.

layers.body: In the General Theory (1936), written amid mass unemployment, Keynes argued economies don't automatically bounce back to full employment. If everyone cuts spending at once, demand collapses and the slump can persist. The cure is to lift total demand — often through government spending.

Output depends on aggregate demand. In bad times fearful households and firms save and hoard cash (a 'liquidity trap'), so private demand won't revive on its own. Government can fill the gap; that spending circulates and multiplies. This justified the post-war welfare state and counter-cyclical policy.

Keynesianism dominated until the 1970s, when 'stagflation' — high inflation and unemployment together — embarrassed the simple models and opened the door to Friedman's monetarism and a free-market revival. It roared back after 2008, when governments again propped up demand. The fight between 'markets self-correct' and 'demand must be managed' never really ends.

cards.detail: Keynes (1936) argued economies can settle below full employment when demand collapses, so government should boost demand in slumps. Dominant until 1970s stagflation, revived after 2008.
cards.deploy: The canonical case for stimulus in a recession — private demand can fail to recover by itself.
cards.counter: Sustained deficit spending can stoke inflation and debt; the 1970s showed demand management has limits.

quiz.q: Keynes argued that in a slump, the economy…
choices: Can stay stuck below full employment

quiz.q: Keynes's prescription for a demand-deficient slump was…
choices: Cut public spending to balance the budget
Government spending to lift aggregate demand
Wait for wages to fall on their own

cards.title: The paradox of thrift
cards.fact: If everyone saves more at once, the country can end up saving less.

layers.body: Saving is wise for one household. But your spending is someone else's income. If everyone tightens their belt at the same time, businesses lose customers, lay people off, and incomes fall — so total saving can actually drop. That's the paradox of thrift.

What's true for one isn't true for all together. Keynes used this to explain why a recession can feed on itself, and why government may need to spend when everyone else is cutting back, to break the downward spiral.

Free-market economists reply that saving funds investment, so thrift isn't wasted — it lowers interest rates and builds future capacity. The paradox bites mainly in a slump with idle resources and rock-bottom rates; in a booming economy, more saving really can mean more investment.

cards.detail: Saving is prudent for one household but, if everyone does it at once in a slump, spending and incomes fall and total saving can drop — a 'fallacy of composition' Keynes used to justify stimulus.
cards.deploy: Explains why 'everyone should just budget like a household' fails for a whole economy at once.
cards.counter: In normal times saving does finance investment; the paradox is a slump phenomenon, not a general law.

cards.title: Friedman and monetarism
cards.fact: Milton Friedman's counter-revolution: inflation is always, everywhere, about money.

layers.body: Friedman led the monetarist challenge to Keynes. His core claim: 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' — too much money chasing too few goods. So control the money supply, not demand, and otherwise let markets work.

With 1970s stagflation discrediting simple Keynesianism, Friedman's Chicago school surged. He argued government 'fine-tuning' does more harm than good, championed floating exchange rates and school vouchers, and reframed the Great Depression as a monetary blunder by the central bank.

Strict monetarism faltered in the 1980s when the link between money supply and inflation proved unstable, and central banks quietly switched from money-supply targets to interest-rate rules. Friedman's broader free-market politics became the orthodoxy of the 'neoliberal' era — credited with taming inflation, blamed by critics for rising inequality and deregulation.

cards.detail: Friedman argued inflation is fundamentally monetary and government meddling does more harm than good. Strict monetarism failed in practice, but his free-market politics shaped the neoliberal era.
cards.deploy: The standard hawkish case that loose money, not greedy sellers, drives inflation.
cards.counter: The money–inflation link is loose in practice; supply shocks and expectations matter, and central banks abandoned strict monetary targets.

cards.title: Hayek and the knowledge problem
cards.fact: Hayek's argument against central planning: nobody knows enough — but prices do.

layers.body: In 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945), Hayek argued the economy's crucial knowledge is scattered across millions of people and never sits in one place, so no planner can gather it. Prices solve this: they quietly compress everyone's local knowledge into a single signal.

A rise in the price of tin tells users worldwide to economise, without anyone explaining why. The market is, for Hayek, a giant information-processing system. This 'knowledge problem' is his deepest case against socialism — not that planners are bad people, but that the task is impossible.

Critics point to where prices carry bad or missing information: pollution and other externalities, monopoly power, advertising, bubbles, and 'lemons' markets where buyers can't judge quality (Akerlof). Prices coordinate brilliantly — and also misfire in ways that can justify regulation. Hayek's insight is real, but not the whole story.

cards.detail: Hayek (1945) argued that dispersed knowledge makes central planning impossible, while prices coordinate it automatically — a deep case for markets that critics qualify with externalities, monopoly and information failures.
cards.deploy: The strongest principled argument against detailed central planning — it's a knowledge problem, not just a motivation one.
cards.counter: Prices routinely get externalities, public goods and information gaps wrong, which is why even market economies regulate.

cards.title: The hockey stick
cards.fact: For most of history, ordinary living standards barely moved. Then, around 1800, they exploded.

layers.body: For millennia, output per person crept along — your distant ancestors lived much like theirs. From the late 1700s in Britain, coal, steam, factories and machines broke that ceiling, and sustained growth in living standards began for the first time in human history.

The 'hockey stick' is the headline of economic history: world output per person was roughly flat for centuries, then rose perhaps ten- to fifteen-fold. Cotton mills, the steam engine and later railways and electricity turned scarcity into mass production. Why it began in Britain — coal, colonies, wages, institutions, science — is hotly argued.

The same revolution brought child labour, brutal hours, slums and environmental wreckage, and its early decades may have squeezed workers' living standards before they rose. It also rested partly on slavery and empire. 'Progress' and 'exploitation' are both true of the same event — which is exactly why it's debated.

cards.detail: After millennia of near-flat living standards, sustained growth began with Britain's Industrial Revolution (~1800), lifting output per person many-fold — at an immense early human and environmental cost.
cards.deploy: Anchors any argument about technology and growth — the modern world is a recent, fragile exception.
cards.counter: The early human costs were immense, and the gains spread very unevenly across people and regions.

quiz.q: The 'hockey stick' of economic history refers to…
choices: Living standards flat for millennia then rising sharply

cards.title: Enclosure and the making of workers
cards.fact: Before there were factory workers, common land had to be fenced off — and people pushed into wage labour.

layers.body: In England, from the 1500s and accelerating into the 1800s, 'enclosure' turned common fields — shared for grazing and farming — into private, fenced property. Many rural people lost access to land they had relied on and had to sell their labour for wages instead.

Enclosure raised farm productivity and helped create a landless workforce — a precondition for the factories of the Industrial Revolution. Marx called this 'primitive accumulation': the often-violent process that turned land and people into capital and labour markets.

Defenders see enclosure as a painful but necessary efficiency gain that fed a growing population and freed labour for industry. Critics see dispossession — a commons taken from the many and handed to the few. How you tell this story shapes how you see capitalism's origins: spontaneous trade, or organised expropriation.

cards.detail: English enclosure (1500s–1800s) privatised common land, creating a wage-dependent workforce — Marx's 'primitive accumulation'. Read either as an efficiency gain or as mass dispossession.
cards.deploy: Reminds us markets in land and labour were created — often by force — not simply 'natural'.
cards.counter: Enclosure also raised food output sharply at a time of rising population; it wasn't pure loss.

cards.title: Bretton Woods and the end of gold
cards.fact: For 27 years the world's money was anchored to gold through the dollar — until one night in 1971 it wasn't.

layers.body: At Bretton Woods (1944) the Allies built the post-war money system: currencies were pegged to the US dollar, and the dollar was convertible to gold at $35 an ounce. It also created the IMF and the World Bank. Stable exchange rates underpinned the post-war boom.

By 1971, US spending meant far more dollars circulated abroad than there was gold to back them. President Nixon suspended gold convertibility — the 'Nixon shock' — and by 1973 major currencies floated freely against each other, as they still do. Money became, finally, purely 'fiat': backed by trust and the state, not metal.

Some see floating money as freedom — countries can run their own monetary policy — and the gold standard as a deflationary straitjacket that worsened the Great Depression. Others (some Austrians, gold bugs) see 1971 as the moment money lost its discipline, enabling chronic inflation and debt. The 'anchor money to something?' debate is alive again in the crypto era.

cards.detail: Bretton Woods (1944) pegged currencies to a gold-backed dollar; Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971 and money became pure fiat. Whether money needs a hard anchor is still argued.
cards.deploy: Background for any argument about fiat money, inflation, gold standards or cryptocurrencies.
cards.counter: Gold standards impose harsh discipline that can deepen depressions; 'sound money' has real costs too.

cards.title: The Great Depression
cards.fact: The 1930s slump was so deep it rewrote economics — and economists still argue about why.

layers.body: After the 1929 Wall Street crash, the US and much of the world fell into the Great Depression: output collapsed and roughly a quarter of American workers lost their jobs. It was the worst downturn of the industrial age and shattered faith in self-correcting markets.

It gave us Keynesian economics and the activist state — the New Deal, public works, financial regulation. The lesson many drew was that markets can stay broken for years, and that government must manage demand and backstop the banks.

Keynes blamed collapsing demand. Friedman and Schwartz blamed the Federal Reserve for letting the money supply shrink as banks failed. Others stress the gold standard, which forced countries to tighten into the slump. Each diagnosis implies a different cure — which is why this one event still shapes how central banks act today.

cards.detail: The 1930s Depression — mass unemployment after the 1929 crash — birthed Keynesianism and the activist state. Its causes (demand collapse, monetary contraction, the gold standard) remain contested.
cards.deploy: Every modern crisis response (2008, 2020) is haunted by 'don't repeat the 1930s'.
cards.counter: There's no settled single cause — demand, money, banking and the gold standard all played a part.

cards.title: The 1970s stagflation
cards.fact: In the 1970s, prices and unemployment rose together — which the textbooks said couldn't happen.

layers.body: Post-war economics assumed a trade-off: more inflation bought less unemployment (the Phillips curve). The 1970s broke it. Oil shocks and other pressures produced 'stagflation' — stagnant growth, high unemployment and high inflation all at once.

The failure discredited the simple Keynesian models and handed the initiative to Friedman's monetarists and the free-market right. Central banks (notably under Volcker in the US) then crushed inflation with brutally high interest rates and a deep recession around 1980, and a new orthodoxy took hold.

Stagflation is the hinge between the Keynesian post-war era and the 'neoliberal' one that followed. Free-marketeers read it as proof that demand management fails and markets must be freed; the left reads the cure — mass unemployment to discipline inflation — as a political choice that shifted power from labour to capital. Same event, opposite lessons.

cards.detail: 1970s stagflation — high inflation and unemployment together — broke the simple Phillips curve, discredited naive Keynesianism, and ushered in monetarism and the free-market turn.
cards.deploy: The go-to counter to naive Keynesianism — and the origin story of modern central banking.
cards.counter: Stagflation was driven heavily by oil shocks; it didn't prove demand management is always wrong.

cards.title: The neoliberal turn
cards.fact: Around 1980, the rich world swung from 'manage the market' to 'free the market'.

layers.body: From the late 1970s, Thatcher in Britain and Reagan in the US led a sharp turn: privatise state firms, cut taxes (especially at the top), deregulate finance, weaken unions, and trust markets over governments. The era is often labelled 'neoliberalism'.

Intellectually it drew on Friedman and Hayek; politically it answered the stagflation crisis of the 1970s. It reshaped the world — globalisation, financial deregulation, and the spread of market reforms from Chile to China to the post-Soviet states. Inflation fell and some economies revived.

Supporters credit it with taming inflation, reviving enterprise and lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty through global trade. Critics blame it for soaring inequality, hollowed-out industry, financial instability culminating in 2008, and eroded public services. 'Neoliberalism' is now used as praise, as a slur, and as a serious analytical term — sometimes in the same argument.

cards.detail: From ~1980, Thatcher and Reagan drove privatisation, tax cuts, deregulation and weaker unions, drawing on Friedman and Hayek. Credited with taming inflation, blamed for inequality and the 2008 crisis.
cards.deploy: Names the framework most current economic arguments are still reacting for or against.
cards.counter: 'Neoliberalism' is a loose label; the period's policies and results varied enormously by country.

cards.title: The 2008 financial crisis
cards.fact: In 2008 the financial system nearly stopped — and the faith that markets police themselves took a beating.

layers.body: A US housing bubble, built on risky mortgages sliced into complex securities, burst and spread through a tightly linked global banking system. Major banks failed or were bailed out, credit froze, and the world fell into the worst recession since the 1930s.

Governments and central banks answered with bank rescues, near-zero interest rates and 'quantitative easing' (creating money to buy assets) — and, at first, Keynesian stimulus. It revived Keynes, dented the strong 'efficient markets' faith that prices always get it right, and exposed how fragile and interconnected modern finance had become.

Still fought over. For some it showed markets need far tighter regulation; for others, that government-backed mortgages and loose central-bank money inflated the bubble in the first place. The turn to austerity after 2010, rather than sustained stimulus, is blamed by Keynesians for a weak recovery and the political backlash that followed.

cards.detail: A 2008 mortgage bubble froze global finance and triggered the worst slump since the 1930s. The bailout-and-stimulus response revived Keynes and dented 'efficient markets' faith; its causes and the later austerity remain contested.
cards.deploy: The modern reference point for financial regulation, bailouts and 'too big to fail'.
cards.counter: Causes are contested — reckless private finance, or government distortions and easy money, or both.
